## Gutenberg in Mainz

Around 1450 to 1455. The 42-line Bible: about 180 copies printed, 49 survive (some only in part). Roughly 135 on paper, 45 on vellum, if I trust the figure on the British Library page. Gutenberg lost the workshop to his backer Johann Fust after the 1455 lawsuit; the record of it, the Helmasperger Notarial Instrument, is in Göttingen. The man who changed everything died more or less broke in 1468.

## Before Gutenberg

Bi Sheng's movable type in Song China, around 1040, described by Shen Kuo. Korea's *Jikji*, 1377, printed with metal type, 78 years before the Bible. With thousands of characters to cast, movable type made less economic sense in East Asia than woodblocks did, which is a useful thing to raise with anyone doing [[Japanese kanji study]]. The Diamond Sutra from Dunhuang (868) is block-printed, see [[Silk Road trade]].

## Dublin's first printed book

1551. The Book of Common Prayer, printed by Humphrey Powell, who had been given £20 by the Privy Council to set up in Dublin. Nothing in Irish type until 1571 (a catechism and an alphabet sheet). The students are always surprised that the first book printed here was in English and was a tool of the Reformation.

## Eisenstein and her critics

Elizabeth Eisenstein, *The Printing Press as an Agent of Change* (CUP, 1979), p. 43: print's big effect was "fixity", identical copies that could be cited, compared and corrected. Adrian Johns, *The Nature of the Book* (1998), pushes back hard: early print was full of piracy and errors, and trust had to be built. I teach both. Fifth years cope fine with "two historians disagree" if you give them one paragraph from each.

## For class

- Luther's 95 Theses, 1517. Something like 300,000 copies of his pamphlets between 1518 and 1525 (number from Pettegree, *Brand Luther*, p. 145).
- Source exercise PP-5Y-03: compare a manuscript page with a printed page of the same text.
- Ask: is the internet more like the press or more like the [[Industrial revolution textiles]] story (cheap copies, jobs lost)?

Related: [[Book club Meditations]], since the first printed Greek text of the *Meditations* only appeared in 1559.
